title: Best Hangover Shots: What's in Them and Which Are Worth It
excerpt: Hangover shots compared: DHM and hovenia shots, ZBiotics, Korean and Japanese drinks, caffeinated shots, DIY ginger and pickle shots, and what actually helps more.
metaDescription: Do hangover shots work? We compare DHM, probiotic, Korean, turmeric, and caffeinated recovery shots, when to take them, and what helps more.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a hangover shot is a small 2-to-3-ounce drink sold to help you feel better after drinking, and none of them is a cure. The better ones are built around ingredients with at least some research behind them, such as DHM or hovenia (the Japanese raisin tree), and they are most useful taken *before or during* drinking, not the morning after. The weaker ones are mostly caffeine, sugar, and B vitamins, which can make you feel more awake without doing anything about why you feel bad. Independent research on finished hangover shots is close to nonexistent, so you are mostly buying the evidence for the ingredients, not the product.

**The quick picks:** For the most plausible formula, choose a DHM or hovenia shot such as Morning Recovery or a Korean shot like Condition, and drink it while you're still drinking. For the most novel idea, ZBiotics is a pre-drinking probiotic shot with a clever mechanism but limited independent proof. For the morning after, a shot won't rehydrate you; a full glass of an electrolyte drink and some food will do more. And if you mainly want DHM, capsules give you more of it for less money than any shot.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide explains published research and the makers' own descriptions of their products. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Hangover shots are sold as foods or dietary supplements. None is approved by the FDA to prevent or treat hangovers, and none lowers your blood alcohol, sobers you up, or makes it safe to drive. **Ask a doctor or pharmacist before using one if** you take prescription medicine (especially blood thinners, diabetes medicine, sedatives, or anti-seizure drugs), are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, or have a heart rhythm problem and the shot contains caffeine. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, or can't be woken up, call 911.

**About our relationships with these brands:** we don't have affiliate arrangements with Morning Recovery, ZBiotics, the Korean and Japanese shot makers, or the caffeinated shot brands, so this page doesn't link to their stores and we earn nothing if you buy them. We do earn a commission on two plain DHM capsule products mentioned near the end, and we say so where they appear.

## What Is a Hangover Shot?

"Hangover shot" covers three quite different things, and it helps to know which one you're looking at before you spend money.

1. **Recovery shots.** Small ready-to-drink bottles, usually 2 to 3.4 ounces, sold in convenience stores, gas stations, and online. These are what most people mean, and they are the focus of this guide.
2. **"Hair of the dog" shots.** A shot of alcohol the next morning to take the edge off. This is a drinking tradition, not a remedy, and we cover why it backfires below.
3. **Injections and IV "shots."** A B12 injection or an IV drip at a hydration clinic, sometimes marketed as a hangover shot. Also covered below.

Within recovery shots, the formulas fall into four rough families:

- **DHM and hovenia shots.** Built around dihydromyricetin (DHM), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, or around extracts of the plant it comes from. This family has the most plausible scientific story.
- **Probiotic shots.** ZBiotics is the main example: an engineered bacterium meant to break down acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol, in your gut.
- **Herbal and liver-support shots.** Turmeric, ginger, milk thistle, prickly pear, and liver extracts, common in Japanese products and in many Western blends.
- **Energy-style shots.** Caffeine, sugar or sweetener, and B vitamins. These make you feel more alert, which is not the same as feeling recovered.

## Why a Small Shot Can Only Do So Much

A hangover isn't one problem. It's several things happening at once: your body dealing with acetaldehyde, low-grade inflammation, poor-quality sleep, fluid loss, irritation of the stomach lining, and swings in blood sugar. Researchers still argue about how much each of these contributes, and the answer probably differs from person to person.

That has two practical consequences for a 3-ounce bottle.

**First, a shot can't rehydrate you.** Alcohol makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. A few ounces of liquid, even with electrolytes in it, is a rounding error next to the fluid you can lose over a night of drinking. If thirst and dry mouth are your main symptoms, a big glass of water or an oral rehydration drink will do more than any shot. Our [electrolyte drink comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) covers which ones are worth buying.

**Second, timing matters more than the label suggests.** Ingredients aimed at alcohol metabolism, like DHM, can only act on alcohol that's still in your system. By the next morning, most of the alcohol is gone and you're dealing with the aftermath. That's why the better-designed shots tell you to drink them during the night or before bed, even when the product name says "morning."

The evidence base for hangover products in general is weak. A 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ* by Pittler, Verster, and Ernst found no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary remedy prevents or treats hangover. A larger 2022 review in the journal *Addiction* (Roberts and colleagues) found that a handful of remedies showed some promise in small trials, but rated the overall quality of the evidence as very low. No hangover shot we know of has strong independent trial data behind the finished product. Keep that in mind when a bottle promises a lot.

## The Best Hangover Shots, Compared

Here's how the main types and best-known products stack up. Formulas change, and many brands sell several versions, so always check the current label.

| Shot | Main active ingredient | When to take it | Strongest point | Biggest weakness |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Morning Recovery (More Labs) | DHM, plus electrolytes and herbal extracts | While drinking or before bed | Most widely sold DHM shot in the US | Modest DHM per bottle; pricey per night |
| ZBiotics | Engineered probiotic (*Bacillus subtilis*) | Before your first drink | Genuinely novel mechanism | Mostly company-run research; most acetaldehyde is made in the liver, not the gut |
| Condition / Morning Care (Korea) | Hovenia (Japanese raisin tree) extract | Before or during drinking | Decades of use; plant is the source of DHM | DHM content rarely listed; mostly sold in Korea |
| Dawn 808 (Korea) | Long proprietary herbal blend | Before or during drinking | Strong word-of-mouth reputation | Hard to know which ingredient, if any, does the work |
| Ukon no Chikara (Japan) | Turmeric (curcumin) | Before drinking | Very widely used in Japan | Weak hangover-specific evidence |
| Caffeinated recovery shots | Caffeine, B vitamins, sugar or sweetener | Morning after | Fast alertness boost | Masks symptoms; caffeine can worsen dehydration jitters and nausea |
| Homemade ginger or pickle-juice shot | Ginger, or sodium from brine | Morning after | Cheap; ginger has real anti-nausea evidence | Small volume; brine is very salty |

## Morning Recovery: The Best-Known DHM Shot

Morning Recovery from More Labs is a small single-serving drink, a little over 3 ounces, and it was one of the first products to put DHM in front of a mainstream US audience. The formula pairs DHM with electrolytes, vitamins, and plant extracts such as milk thistle and prickly pear. More Labs has sold several versions over the years, including a zero-sugar one.

**Pros:**

- Built around DHM, the ingredient in this category with the most interesting research.
- Designed to be taken during drinking or before bed, which matches how DHM is thought to work.
- Convenient and easy to find in stores and online.

**Cons:**

- The amount of DHM per bottle is modest compared with a typical DHM capsule dose.
- Expensive per night compared with plain DHM.
- No published clinical trial of the finished drink that we're aware of.

**Who it suits:** people who like the ritual of a bottle and want something they'll actually remember to drink before bed. For more detail, see our [full Morning Recovery review](/never-hungover/more-labs-morning-recovery-review).

## ZBiotics: The Probiotic Pre-Drinking Shot

ZBiotics calls itself a "pre-alcohol probiotic." It's a small drink containing a strain of *Bacillus subtilis* that the company engineered to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde. You drink it before your first alcoholic drink.

**Pros:**

- A clever, specific mechanism rather than a pile of vitamins.
- *B. subtilis* is a common food bacterium, and the product is low-risk for most healthy adults.
- Simple to use: one bottle, before drinking.

**Cons:**

- Most acetaldehyde is made in your liver, not your gut, which limits how much a gut probiotic can logically do.
- Scientists still disagree about how much acetaldehyde drives the hangover you feel the next day.
- The research behind it is mostly the company's own, and many users report they can't tell a difference.

**Who it suits:** the curious drinker who doesn't mind the cost and wants to test something new. Our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) goes deeper into the science.

## Korean Hangover Shots: Condition, Morning Care, and Dawn 808

In South Korea, small hangover drinks (called *haejang* drinks) sit by the register in almost every convenience store, and many people drink one before a work dinner. The two biggest brands, Condition and Morning Care, are built around **hovenia extract**, from the same Japanese raisin tree that DHM is extracted from. Dawn 808 takes a different approach, with a long proprietary list of herbal ingredients.

**Pros:**

- Hovenia has a plausible link to hangover relief because it contains DHM.
- Decades of widespread use with a good general safety record in healthy adults.
- Designed to be taken before drinking, which is the right timing.

**Cons:**

- Labels usually don't say how much DHM is in the hovenia extract, so you can't compare doses.
- The few human studies are small and often connected to the manufacturers.
- Outside Korea, you'll usually find them only in Asian grocery stores or through importers.

Our [guide to Korean and Japanese hangover pills and drinks](/never-hungover/korean-japanese-hangover-pills) compares each brand in detail, and our piece on [Korean pear juice for hangovers](/never-hungover/korean-pear-juice-hangover) covers the other popular Korean option.

## Japanese Turmeric Shots: Ukon no Chikara

Japan's best-known hangover shot is Ukon no Chikara, a small canned or bottled drink built on **turmeric** (*ukon* in Japanese). Many people drink one before a night out.

**Pros:**

- Very widely used, with a long track record as a food product.
- Turmeric is low-risk at food-like amounts for most healthy adults.

**Cons:**

- The case for turmeric against hangovers specifically is weaker than the case for hovenia or DHM. Curcumin is also poorly absorbed by the body on its own.
- Turmeric supplements can interact with blood thinners, and high-dose turmeric products have been linked to rare cases of liver injury. If you take a blood thinner or have liver or gallbladder disease, check with a doctor first.

## Caffeinated Recovery Shots

A separate group of shots, sold at gas stations and in party-supply aisles, is essentially an energy shot with a hangover label. Hangover Joe's is the best-known US example. These usually combine caffeine with B vitamins and sugar or a sweetener.

**Pros:**

- Caffeine really does make you feel more alert, and if you're a daily coffee drinker, it can head off a caffeine-withdrawal headache layered on top of your hangover.
- Cheap and easy to find.

**Cons:**

- Feeling more awake isn't the same as recovering. Caffeine does nothing for acetaldehyde, inflammation, or lost sleep.
- On an empty, irritated stomach, a concentrated dose of caffeine can make nausea and jitteriness worse, and it can push up your heart rate when it may already be elevated after drinking.
- Never use an energy shot *while* drinking. Mixing caffeine with alcohol makes you feel less drunk than you are, which tends to lead to drinking more.

**Who it suits:** a regular coffee drinker who needs to function in the morning and would have had caffeine anyway. A cup of coffee with breakfast does the same job for less.

## DIY Hangover Shots: Ginger, Pickle Juice, and Lemon

You can make a "hangover shot" at home for very little money, and two of the common versions have a sensible rationale.

**Ginger shots.** Ginger has real evidence for easing nausea, though most of it comes from morning sickness, motion sickness, and post-surgery nausea rather than hangovers. Around 1 gram of ginger is roughly what nausea studies used. A straight ginger shot is spicy and acidic, so on a raw stomach, sipped ginger tea may go down more easily. See our [guide to ginger for hangovers](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) for amounts and forms.

**Pickle juice shots.** Pickle brine is mostly water, vinegar, and a lot of sodium. The salt can help your body hold on to fluid, which is the logic behind it. The catch is that a single shot can carry a large share of a day's recommended sodium, so it's not a good choice if you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, and it can be rough on an already irritated stomach.

**Lemon, honey, and cayenne shots.** These are popular on social media. Honey gives you a little sugar, which may help if your blood sugar is low, and the rest is mostly flavor. There's no good evidence that cayenne or lemon does anything for a hangover.

The honest limit of every DIY shot is the same as the bottled ones: a couple of ounces can't replace the fluid, food, and sleep your body actually needs.

## What About "Hair of the Dog" Shots?

A shot of vodka or a Bloody Mary the morning after can make you feel better for an hour or two. That's real, and it's the reason the tradition survives. But it works by giving your body more alcohol to deal with, which postpones the hangover rather than ending it. You're adding more acetaldehyde and more fluid loss to a system that's already behind.

There's another reason to be wary. If you regularly need a drink in the morning to stop shaking, sweating, or feeling anxious, that's not an ordinary hangover. Those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, and withdrawal can become dangerous. It's worth talking to a doctor plainly about it; they can help you stop safely.

## What About B12 Shots and IV Hangover Drips?

Some clinics and "mobile IV" services sell B12 injections or IV drips as hangover shots, often with vitamins, electrolytes, and anti-nausea medicine.

- **B12 injections:** there is no good evidence that a B12 shot helps a hangover in someone who isn't deficient in B12. Alcohol doesn't drain your B12 in one night.
- **IV fluids:** fluids through a vein do rehydrate you quickly, and anti-nausea medicine added to a drip can genuinely help if you're vomiting. But for a typical hangover where you can keep liquids down, drinking fluids gets you to the same place for a fraction of the cost.

If you're vomiting so much you can't keep any fluids down, that's a reason to see a doctor or urgent care, not to book a wellness drip.

## How to Choose a Hangover Shot

If you want to try one, these questions will get you to a sensible choice:

1. **When will you take it?** If the answer is "the next morning," skip the shot and focus on water, an electrolyte drink, food, and a painkiller if appropriate. Shots built around DHM or hovenia need to go in while alcohol is still in your system.
2. **Does the label tell you how much of the active ingredient is in it?** A clear dose ("DHM 300 mg") is a good sign. "Proprietary blend" means you can't compare products.
3. **How much caffeine is in it?** Avoid caffeinated shots during drinking, and be careful with them if you're sensitive to caffeine or have a heart rhythm problem.
4. **How much sugar?** Some shots carry a surprising amount of sugar for their size. That matters if you have diabetes or are watching your intake.
5. **What does it cost per night?** Single bottles are often several times the cost of a capsule serving of the same ingredient.
6. **Does it interact with anything you take?** Turmeric, ginger, and some herbal blends can interact with blood thinners. Ask a pharmacist if you take daily medicine.

## Shots vs. Capsules: Which Is Better Value?

For most people, the honest answer is capsules. The ingredient with the most promising research in this category is DHM. Early animal research, including a 2012 study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues, found that DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal in rats. Human data is still limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone. But if DHM is what you're after, a capsule gives you a clearer dose and a much lower cost per night than a shot.

Shots win on convenience and ritual. Some people simply remember to drink a bottle before bed more reliably than they remember to take a pill. If that's you, a DHM shot is a reasonable choice. If cost or dose matters more, capsules make more sense. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our overview of [whether hangover pills actually work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-pills-actually-work) covers the rest of the category.

## What Helps More Than Any Shot

Whatever you buy, these habits do more of the work:

- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
- **Alternate drinks with water,** and have a big glass before bed.
- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, and nothing in a bottle speeds that up.
- **Protect your sleep.** Alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night, which is a big part of why you feel wrecked.
- **The morning after,** drink fluids, eat something gentle (our post on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains why breakfast helps), and use a painkiller only if it's safe for you.

## When to See a Doctor

> **Get medical help if:** you can't keep fluids down for several hours; you're vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds; you have severe stomach pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, chest pain, or confusion; or your symptoms are getting worse after a day instead of better. **Call 911 for signs of alcohol poisoning:** confusion, vomiting while drowsy, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, bluish or pale skin, or someone who can't be woken up. And if you find yourself needing a drink in the morning to stop shaking or sweating, tell a doctor. That can be alcohol withdrawal, and a doctor can help you manage it safely.

## The Bottom Line

The best hangover shots are the ones built around DHM or hovenia and taken while you're still drinking. Morning Recovery and the Korean hovenia shots fit that description, and ZBiotics is an interesting experiment with an unusual mechanism. Caffeinated shots make mornings feel more manageable but don't change how your body is recovering. And no shot of any kind replaces food, water, pacing, and sleep.

If you mainly want DHM, capsules are the better value. Two we link to (and earn a commission on) are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a plain 1,000 mg DHM capsule with a low cost per serving, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which pairs DHM with L-cysteine and other ingredients. Neither is a cure, and there is no good evidence that any supplement lets you drink heavily without consequences. They're simply a cheaper way to get the ingredient the better shots are built on. For a ranked list of bottled options, see our [best hangover recovery drinks guide](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best hangover shot?**

The most sensible choices are shots built around DHM or hovenia (the Japanese raisin tree), such as Morning Recovery or Korean shots like Condition, taken while you're still drinking or before bed. ZBiotics is a reasonable experiment if you're curious about its probiotic approach. No shot has strong independent trial evidence behind the finished product, and none is a cure.

**Do hangover shots actually work?**

Maybe a little, for some people, but no one has shown it in a controlled trial. Reviews of hangover remedies, including a 2005 BMJ review and a 2022 review in the journal Addiction, found little high-quality evidence for any product. Shots built on DHM or hovenia have the most plausible mechanism. Caffeinated shots make you feel more alert without addressing why you feel bad.

**When should you drink a hangover shot?**

For DHM, hovenia, and probiotic shots, take them before or during drinking, or right before bed, while alcohol is still in your system. By the next morning, most of the alcohol is gone and these ingredients have little left to act on. Caffeinated shots are meant for the morning after and should never be mixed with alcohol.

**Is a hangover shot better than DHM capsules?**

Not usually on value. Capsules give a clearer DHM dose at a much lower cost per night. Shots win on convenience, and some people find a bottle easier to remember before bed. If DHM is the ingredient you want, capsules are the cheaper way to get it.

**Does a shot of alcohol cure a hangover?**

No. A "hair of the dog" shot can make you feel better for a short time, but it does that by adding more alcohol, which delays the hangover rather than ending it. If you regularly need a drink in the morning to stop shaking or sweating, talk to a doctor, because that can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal.

**Do B12 shots help a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that a B12 injection helps a hangover unless you're actually deficient in B12. IV drips do rehydrate you quickly, but if you can keep fluids down, drinking water or an electrolyte drink gets you to the same place for much less money. If you can't keep any fluids down, see a doctor or urgent care.

**Are hangover shots safe?**

Most are low-risk for healthy adults when used as directed. Check the label for caffeine and sugar, and ask a pharmacist first if you take blood thinners, diabetes medicine, sedatives, or other daily prescriptions, since ingredients like turmeric and ginger can interact. No hangover shot lowers your blood alcohol or makes it safe to drive.

**Do Korean hangover drinks work?**

Korean drinks like Condition and Morning Care are built on hovenia extract, the plant DHM comes from, which gives them a plausible rationale. The human studies are small and often linked to the makers, and labels rarely say how much DHM they contain. They're a reasonable thing to try before drinking, alongside food and water.
